query: Earlier studies of conventional metallic multilayers provide a general framework for deformation, but its conclusions may not transfer directly to high-entropy-alloy systems because compositional complexity, severe lattice distortion, and short-range order are associated with unusual deformation behavior. Preliminary evidence from FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers remains insufficient to establish what controls creep or when a given response dominates. Within the constraints of retaining a nanoscale multilayer coating and balancing strength with deformation tolerance, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading? State what governs the behavior and why, an unspecified controlled comparison that would expose it, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, boundary conditions, relevant prior support, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Under sustained loading, the progressive plastic deformation (creep) in FCC/BCC high‐entropy-alloy nanoscale multilayers is controlled by the evolution of interface-mediated chemical short-range order (SRO). Initially, the SRO at the interfaces between layers impedes dislocation motion and strengthens the multilayer. However, as sustained stress disrupts this SRO, dislocation nucleation and glide are facilitated, resulting in an accelerated creep rate.
generation.material_initial_state: Nanoscale multilayer coatings composed of alternating FCC and BCC high-entropy alloy layers with significant lattice distortion and well-developed chemical short-range order at their interfaces.
generation.intervention: Systematically vary the individual layer thickness and/or fine-tune the layer compositions to either enhance or suppress the initial SRO at the layer interfaces.
generation.conditions: Creep tests under sustained, constant stress at an elevated temperature that activates creep without degrading the multilayer structure (representative of service conditions where both strength and ductility are important).
generation.structural_mediator: Interface-localized chemical short-range order (SRO) that is sensitive to compositional variations and lattice distortions.
generation.mechanism: The initial SRO at layer interfaces acts as a barrier to dislocation motion, providing high strength. Under sustained stress, this ordered structure begins to degrade; the loss of SRO reduces barrier strength, enabling easier dislocation nucleation and glide. This transition leads to a progressive increase in creep strain, particularly pronounced in thinner layers where interfaces dominate the microstructure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to baseline multilayers with optimal layer thickness and composition, specimens with thinner layers (or compositions engineered for stronger initial SRO) will exhibit a relatively higher creep rate over time due to a more rapid degradation of SRO and subsequent increase in dislocation activity.
generation.baseline: Multilayer specimens with balanced layer thickness and compositions that maintain a stable interface SRO and show moderate creep rates under the same stress and temperature conditions.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold under intermediate elevated temperatures and stresses that promote atomic diffusion and dislocation activity while keeping the multilayer architecture intact. At very low temperatures (minimal atomic mobility) or very high temperatures (where complete structural degradation or alternate deformation mechanisms may dominate), the mechanism may not be the primary control factor.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative aspects such as the exact rate of SRO degradation or its direct correlation with dislocation activation energies remain uncertain. Moreover, potential secondary mechanisms (e.g., phase transformation at interfaces) might also contribute under different conditions, warranting further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate a series of HEA multilayers with systematically varied layer thicknesses and compositional modifications designed to alter the initial degree of interface SRO. Subject these samples to identical sustained stress–temperature creep tests while performing in situ or ex situ microstructural characterization (using techniques such as TEM diffraction, atom-probe tomography, or synchrotron-based methods) to monitor both dislocation behavior and the evolution of interface SRO.
measurements: Creep strain vs. time curves to determine creep rate
Dislocation density and spatial distribution via TEM
Interface SRO characterization (e.g., via atom probe or diffraction techniques)
Variation in layer thickness and compositional uniformity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the specimens with engineered higher initial SRO (or thinner layers) do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in creep rate or if no correlation between SRO degradation and enhanced dislocation activity is observed relative to the baseline multilayers, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

In particular, refractory MPEA (RMPEA) shows high strength at elevated temperatures (), but its low room-temperature ductility hinders the wide applications (). Recently, non-screw dislocation slip plays an important contribution to plastic deformation in RMPEA () and attracts a lot of great attention to break through this dilemma (). Additionally, the differences of the electronic interactions lead to the existence of preference or avoidance in the atom bonding and then produce chemical short-range order (SRO) to reduce the free energy of the system confirmed by experiments (). Considering the fact that stacking fault, twinning, and phase transformation are the dislocation-mediated process (, ), the SRO-induced non-uniform lattice strain fields result in unusual dislocation behavior for the excellent performance compared to traditional alloys (, ). The mechanical properties of high-entropy alloys are receiving continuous attention as they combine excellent strength with ductility,. One of the microscopic origins of their features lies in the slow dislocation activity in these alloys, that is caused by the lattice distortion brought about by the mix of atomic constituents with various sizes. Recently, high-entropy alloys forming single-phase bcc crystals have come into the focus of research. Among them, the equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy has become one of the best investigated examples; it is also known as the Senkov alloy. Thus, Xu et al. directly model the shear strength of the HfNbTaTiZr alloy and observe failure by a bcc-to-fcc phase transformation initiating in HfTi rich regions. Liang et al. study how variable fractions of Hf and Ta in HfNbTaTiZr alloys affect the tensile strength. Recently, Hf15Nb40Ta25Ti15Zr15 was found to be both strong and ductile at cryogenic to elevated temperatures. Due to the chemical complexity of these concentrated alloys, the local stoichiometry may deviate from the overall composition leading to local chemical short-range order. In summary, the study reveals that the maximum strength and critical grain size can be manipulated by tuning the degree of chemical SRO, signifying the nontrivial role of local chemical ordering on the ultimate strength of MPEAs. As the salient feature of MPEAs, the presence of SRO considerably affects deformation microstructure and local plastic strain, originating from its effects on SF energy increase and diffuse antiphase boundary development. As a result, the volume fracture of deformation hcp atoms is decreased to compensate the increased SF energy, and plastic strain is more localized to embrace slip-mediated SRO destruction and glide plane softening. The crystal orientation of constituent grains plays a vital role in deformation mechanisms, microstructure evolution, and dislocation patterning, which collectively affect the mechanical behavior of individual grains and, hence, system-level performance.
